summary: Provides examples of S/MIME messages, including Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) objects and the MIME formatting around them. The goal is to help implementers test and improve interoperability for S/MIME and other protocols that use CMS. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When learning a new recipe, a picture of the finished dish helps. This memo shows finished examples of secure email messages so people building software can check their work.

subtitle: Real-world examples of cryptographic email messages for testing and interoperability

tldr.problem: Developers building S/MIME and CMS implementations need concrete examples to test their code and ensure interoperability with other implementations.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a comprehensive collection of example S/MIME messages and CMS objects, including signed messages, encrypted messages, and various certificate formats, all with step-by-step breakdowns of their structure.
tldr.outcome: These verified examples help implementers validate their code and improve compatibility, making it easier to build email security features that work across different systems.

today: RFC 4134 remains an informational reference for S/MIME and CMS implementers. As an example document, it has not been obsoleted and continues to be used for testing and validation of email security implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4134 provides examples of message bodies formatted using S/MIME (Secure Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) and CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) objects. The goal is to help implementers build and test email security systems, especially by ensuring different implementations can understand each other's messages. The RFC covers many common CMS formats, from simple data containers to complex signed and encrypted messages.

Every example in the document has been checked by two different implementers, which provides strong (though not absolute) confidence that the examples are correct. The examples date back many years and were created and validated by different people over time, so some certificate lifespans and dates in the examples are quite old. Implementers should not use these examples as stand-alone explanations of how to create CMS messages, but rather as references for testing and validation.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is like a cookbook of real email security examples. Each recipe has been tested by two chefs to make sure it works.

sections.title: Constants and Building Blocks
sections.content:
The RFC defines standard building blocks used across all examples: sample content, private keys, certificates, and certificate revocation lists (CRLs). The sample content is a simple sentence ("This is some sample content."), but all examples show its exact binary representation and cryptographic hashes (MD5 and SHA-1).

The examples use fictional characters (Alice, Bob, Carl, Diane, and Erica) to represent different roles: signers, recipients, and certificate authorities. Private keys are provided for different signature algorithms (DSS and RSA) and encryption keys. Certificates include extensions for key usage, subject alternative names, and chain-of-trust validation. CRLs (lists of revoked certificates) are also included in various forms.
sections.plainLanguage: Before cooking, you set up your ingredients and tools. Here, the examples set up pretend people with fake keys and certificates so you can see exactly how they are used.

sections.title: Signed and Encrypted Messages
sections.content:
The RFC covers several major CMS content types. SignedData is the format for digitally signed messages, shown with different signature algorithms (DSS and RSA), with and without attributes, and with multiple signers. Some examples include detached signatures (where the content is not included in the signed structure) and S/MIME multipart formats that wrap the signature in MIME headers.

EnvelopedData is the format for encrypted messages, shown with different encryption algorithms (TripleDES and RC2). DigestedData and EncryptedData are less common formats also covered. Each example shows the exact byte-for-byte structure of the message in a readable decoded format, making it possible to verify implementations against a known good example.
sections.plainLanguage: The main kinds of secure messages are ones you sign (proving it is from you) and ones you encrypt (so only the right person can read them). This section shows real examples of both.

sections.title: Message Structure and Format
sections.content:
Each example in the RFC is presented in two ways: first as a human-readable breakdown of the binary structure, then in appendices as actual encoded binary data. The readable breakdown uses standard notation to show the nesting of data structures, field lengths, object identifiers, and content values.

The RFC includes an extraction program (referenced in Appendix A) that shows how to parse the binary examples and verify them. This allows implementers to take the raw encoded data, decode it with their own implementation, and check that the output matches the expected structure shown in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each example is shown in two ways: first as a readable map of what is where, then as the actual bits and bytes. It is like showing a building blueprint and then the building itself.

sections.title: Testing and Interoperability
sections.content:
The primary use of this RFC is for testing. An implementer can take the binary examples and feed them to their S/MIME or CMS parser to verify that it correctly decodes and validates them. The RFC also serves as a troubleshooting reference: if two implementations disagree on how to interpret a message, the RFC provides a correct reference point.

The document also covers edge cases and variations that might not be obvious from the abstract specification in other RFCs. For instance, it shows how different certificate paths, attribute handling, and signature formats can all appear in real messages. This makes it valuable for developers who need to handle the full range of real-world messages, not just the simple cases.
sections.plainLanguage: If your email software is broken, you can test it against the examples here to see what is wrong. It is like a practice test that tells you the right answers.
